rows.speaker: Ebussuud
rows.claim: Ebussuud treats the three occurrences of people as the same, repeated for clarification, emphasis, and to dignify humanity.
rows.anchor: insanlık şerefini tezyid için tekrar olunmuştur. Demek olur ki Ebussuud da bunu ihtiyar eylemiştir

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Âlûsî prefers the same referent each time, following the usual rule that a definite noun repeated is identical to its first occurrence.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî de “bir şeyin ma‘rife olarak i‘âdesi hâlinde, ikinci evvelin aynı olmak” kā‘ide-i ekseriyesine binâen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers a distinct sense for each occurrence: exact repeated endings are unexpected, the apposition concerns Lord, and each possessive relation gives a different sense; the identity rule applies only without contrary evidence.
rows.anchor: her birinde muzâf-ı ileyhin muzâfına göre başkaca bir mâna beyan etmiş olması daha doğru ve daha fâidelidir

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ ve bazı ârifîn
rows.claim: They describe the soul as initially empty of acquired knowledge but naturally capable of knowing and loving God, then progressing through first principles and inferential capacity to actualized theoretical knowledge.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ ve bazı ârifîn demişlerdir ki: “Zira nefs-i insânî asıl fıtrafında ma‘rifetullah ve mahabbetullah ile intikāşa müsta‘iddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author maps the soul's initial ignorance, capacity for inference, and perfected actual knowledge respectively to Lord, King, and God, presenting three divine modes of governance.
rows.anchor: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ nefs-i insânî merâtibinden ilk mertebeye işarettir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Râzî says Lord comes first as the one who nurtures and reforms; once a person gains reason and sees himself as owned by his Lord, he recognizes God as King, then as the sole object of worship.
rows.anchor: Râzî Felak Sûresi’nde bunu nakletmekle beraber burada bu farkı şöyle hulâsa eder: “Evvelâ ‘rabb’i zikr ile başlamıştır

rows.speaker: Beyzâvî
rows.claim: Beyzâvî reads the sequence as both the seeker's stages of recognizing a Creator from blessings, then the true sovereign, then the sole one worthy of worship, and the customary escalation from tutor to ruler to King of kings.
rows.anchor: Beyzâvî de bunu şöyle ifade etmiştir: “Bu nazm-ı celîlde O Rabb’in sığınmaya lâyık i‘âzeye kādir

rows.speaker: Bazıları
rows.claim: Some distinguish the three human groups as infants needing nurture, youths and adults needing governance, and worshippers and mature people devoted to God.
rows.anchor: Bazıları tekrar olmadığını anlatmak için daha sade olarak şöyle demişlerdir: “İlk nâs cenîn ve etfâl gibi terbiyeye muhtaç olanlar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the proposed distinctions are all significant and broadly compatible, whether framed philosophically, rhetorically, or simply.
rows.anchor: bu gösterilen farkların hepsi de mühim ve şâyân-ı dikkattir. Bazısı daha felsefî, bazısı daha edebî, bazısı da sade

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lord derives from nurture, whose right depends on ownership; because nurture applies to rational and non-rational beings, Lord is the broadest title and people here means all humanity.
rows.anchor: terbiye hakkı da mâlikiyete[^30] mütevakkıf bulunmak itibariyle zevi’l-ukūlden olanlara da olmayanlara da ta‘alluk ettiği için e‘amdır

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Râgıb says mulk denotes command and prohibition over the public and political direction of rational beings, so one says King of people, not King of things.
rows.anchor: Râgıb der ki: [6418] “‘Mîm’in zammıyla ‘mülk’, cumhur üzerinde emr ü nehy ile tasarruftur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because kingship concerns governing rational people, people under the title King means the rational portion of humanity and is narrower than the first occurrence.
rows.anchor: Şu hâlde “meliki’n-nâs”daki “nâs” ale’l-umûm insan cinsi içinden aklı eren insanlar olmak lâzım gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divinity denotes the highest perfection and entitlement to worship with deepest love and reverence; its people are humans possessing some maturity in reason, conscience, faith, character, and conduct.
rows.anchor: En derin sevgi, en yüksek tâzim ile ibadete istihkākı ifade eden ilâhlık, hak tanrılık ise ekmel-i sıfât olduğundan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first occurrence encompasses everyone, including fetuses and children, since no person is ever independent of divine nurture; it does not restrict the verse to beginners.
rows.anchor: henüz ilk terbiyeye muhtaç ve akıl melekesi husûle gelmemiş cenin ve etfâl gibiler dahi dâhil olmak üzere lâm-ı istiğrak ile ale’l-umûm insanlar cinsine şâmil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although people can mean common folk disparagingly, the honor conveyed by its attachment to Lord rules out contempt here, and there is no contextual basis for narrowing its universal scope.
rows.anchor: burada tahkir kasdına münâfî olacağından, bunun muktezâsı olan ta‘mîmi tahsîse karîne yoktur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apposition identifies the referent rather than defining a word's concept, as in Abu Hafs meaning Umar.
rows.anchor: Ancak atf-ı beyanda asıl maksud mefhûmu beyan değil, mâsadakı[^32], müsemmâyı beyandır

rows.speaker: Ebû Hayyân
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that apposition characteristically uses a fixed proper name rather than a descriptive adjective.
rows.anchor: Ve onun için Ebû Hayyân “atf-ı beyanda meşhur olan sıfat ile değil, ism-i câmidle olmaktır” diye Keşşâf’a ilişmiştir

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi answers that these divine names function here like fixed names, so they can serve as apposition rather than descriptions.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî de buradakilerin ism-i câmid hükmünde olduğu beyânıyla ona cevap vermiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second and third people need be neither wholly identical with nor wholly different from the first; each is considered in relation to the narrower divine title that names God's essence.
rows.anchor: burada ma‘nâ-yı murâda intikal için vasfiyet mânasıyla izâfetin beyanda âlet-i mülâhaza gibi tasavvuruna ihtiyaç bulunduğu da inkâr edilemez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second occurrence conventionally encompasses rational adults whose capacities and conflicts require political direction, protection, justice, and cooperative social order.
rows.anchor: küçük büyük gelmiş geçmiş ve gelecek ale’l-umûm insan cinsi üzerinde rubûbiyeti cârî olan tek rab, ve böyle bütün âkil bâliğ insanlar üzerinde mülkü

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The King over all rational adults across past, present, and future cannot be a human or any other created being.
rows.anchor: mülkü, melekûtu hâkim ve dâim tek melik

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third people are perfected believers: prophets, the truthful, martyrs, righteous, and sincere believing men and women who seek to follow and be gathered with them.
rows.anchor: bu üçüncü “nâs” âkil insanlar içinden enbiyâ ve sıddîkīn ve şühedâ ve sâlihîn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are the people promised protection, associated with those blessed in the Opening and the guided, successful believers at the beginning of al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: Hakikaten sığındırılıp korunmaları vaad olunanlar da bunlardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three modes of humanity also recall the stages of revival, death, and resurrection for final return described in other verses.
rows.anchor: nâsın böyle rubûbiyet, mülk, ilâhiyet hükümleri tahtında birer âyette üç tavır ile iadesi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names can mark humanity's passage from lifeless matter to life under God's nurture, then life and death under His rule, then resurrection and judgment under His divinity.
rows.anchor: İnsanlar emvât iken yani hayatsız arz, câmid madde, ölü toprak iken onları rubûbiyeti hükmüyle ihyâ edip insan yapan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking refuge also means voluntary repentance and return before the inevitable forced return, drawing near through supererogatory worship toward abiding in God.
rows.anchor: her emrine âmâde olmak üzere rücû‘-i ihtiyârî demek olan tevbe ve inâbe ile

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sacred report promises that the servant keeps drawing near through extra devotions until God becomes his hearing, sight, and heart; this is the practical result of the Fatiha covenant and great success.
rows.anchor: لاَ يـَزَالُ الْعَبْدُ يـَتـَقَرَّبُ إِلَيَّ بِالنـَّوَافِلِ حَتَّى أَكُونَ سَمْعَهُ وَبَصَرَهُ وَقـَلْبَهُ hadîs-i kudsîsi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Falaq invokes one attribute against three kinds of harm, whereas this surah invokes three attributes against one evil, showing whispering is more dangerous and refuge matters especially at life's end.
rows.anchor: isti‘âze olunan ise bir şerdir. Demek ki bu şer, bu âfet evvelki âfetlerin hepsinden büyük

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The praise offered in seeking refuge should match the gravity of the danger for which help is sought.
rows.anchor: demek ki isti‘âze için senâ dahi, istenilen matlûbun kadrine göre olmak îcâb eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: External harms do not penetrate or stain a person's soul or make that person accountable absent causal involvement in thought, belief, or choice; suffering them can earn reward.
rows.anchor: onda insanın kendi düşüncesinden, itikādından, iradesinden, kesbinden bir sebebiyet bulunmadıkça, o şey onun hakikatine nüfuz etmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evil arising within a person, or induced with some consent, is that person's own accountable evil and makes the soul its own enemy.
rows.anchor: kendi şerridir, o ondan mes’uldür; rûhunu kirletmiş kendi kendine düşmanlık etmiş olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul's worst affliction is inward corruption—disbelief, weak resolve, bad judgment, harmful impulses, deception, and doubt—summed up as whispering.
rows.anchor: Nefs-i insânînin en büyük âfeti işte böyle kendi içinden gelen fenalık, içindeki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited couplet says inward afflictions, rather than a bare wound, are the source of calamity.
rows.anchor: Mecrûhu sanma cerh-i mücerreddir öldüren Âfât-ı bâtıniyedir aslı musibetin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an opens by establishing faith and certainty about the afterlife as conditions of success, and closes by commanding refuge from the stealthy whisper that drives every evil.
rows.anchor: Kur’ân’ın evvelinde reybi nefy ile iman ve âhirete îkān korunmanın, felâhın ilk şartı olarak tesbit edildiği gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means seeking refuge from the evil of the retreating, stealthy whisperer who repeatedly deceives and pushes people back from God's path.
rows.anchor: geri geri çekilip sinen, sinip sinip aldatmak, Hak yolundan geriletip fenalığa sürüklemek için döne döne vesvese

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waswas is a verbal noun or infinitive, also used intensively as an adjective or name for a frequent whisperer, virtually a source of whispering.
rows.anchor: mübalağa için sıfat ve isim olarak kullanılmıştır ki ayn-ı vesvese kesilmiş, vesvese kaynağı demek gibidir

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: Kashshaf says the definite al-waswas became a name for Satan because whispering and misleading are his constant work.
rows.anchor: Keşşâf’ın dediği gibi bütün şuğlü, san‘atı ve dâima üzerine düştüğü hep vesvese ve iğvâdır

rows.speaker: Ebû Hayyân
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says waswas can also mean the whispering of desires, that is, the forbidden prompting of the lower self.
rows.anchor: Bahr’da Ebû Hayyân der ki: “‘el-vesvâs’ Şeytan’ın ismi demişlerdir

rows.speaker: Keşşâf ve Râgıb
rows.claim: They explain waswasa as a faint, hidden sound or whisper, like a hiss or private murmur.
rows.anchor: Keşşâf’ın ve Râgıb’ın da söyledikleri vechile “vesvese” esasen “fis, hiş” demek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word extended from faint sounds, including jewelry rustling and hunters' or dogs' quiet sounds, to evil and worthless thoughts cast into the heart by the self or Satan.
rows.anchor: huliyyât hışıltısına, “vesvâsü’l-huliy” denilmesi bundandır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses the verb for both the soul's whispering and Satan's whispering.
rows.anchor: âyeti nefsin vesvesesi hakkında

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hannas is an intensive active participle or related form from hunus, modifying waswas and describing habitual retreat or concealment.
rows.anchor: “Hunûs”tan mübalağalı ism-i fâil veya o vezinde ism-i mensûb olarak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunus covers withdrawal, return, contraction, disappearance, and—transitively—making something retreat, shrink, or vanish.
rows.anchor: lâzım olarak teahhur ve rücû‘, yani gerilemek ve geri dönmek, ve inkıbaz ve gaybûbet

rows.speaker: Müfessirîn ekseriyetle
rows.claim: Most exegetes explain hannas from the intransitive sense: one who withdraws or contracts, then returns when an opportunity comes.
rows.anchor: Müfessirîn ekseriyetle lâzımdan teahhur ve inkıbaz ile sinmek mânasını esas tutarak tefsir eylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: Kashshaf cites Sa'id ibn Jubayr: Satan retreats when a person remembers God and returns to whisper when that person becomes heedless.
rows.anchor: Keşşâf’ta: “Hunûsa mensûb, âdeti hunûs yani teahhur etmek olandır

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Raghib defines hannas as Satan, who contracts when God is remembered.
rows.anchor: Râgıb da der ki: “‘Hannâs’ hunûs eden, yani Allah anıldığı zaman munkabız olan şeytandır

rows.speaker: Ebû Hayyân
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan extends the term to Satan and the passions: Satan withdraws at remembrance, while desires shrink through faith, angelic inspiration, and shame; the phrase may include human selves or evil companions.
rows.anchor: Ebû Hayyân bunun nefse de şümûlünü ve tam sinsilik mânasını göstererek Bahr’da demiştir ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the transitive sense, hannas means one who makes people regress or shrink from faith, certainty, patience, resolve, and good works toward animal pleasures and deceit.
rows.anchor: Şeytan ve şehevât hakkında bu da doğrudur, çünkü bunlar vesveseleriyle insanı geriletir, insanlık rûhunu hak yolunda terakkiden alıkor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whisperer recedes when God is remembered or feared, then returns with opportunity and gradually humiliates its victim through insinuations; the author therefore favors translating hannas as stealthy.
rows.anchor: Allah anıldıkça, Hak korkusu göründükçe geriler, siner, fırsat buldukça döner, yüz buldukça şımarır

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina identifies waswas with the imaginative faculty: it activates the animal soul and turns it away from its proper orientation toward immaterial principles.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ demiş[^55] ki: “‘Vesvâs’ vesvese îkā‘eden kuvvedir

rows.speaker: Bazıları
rows.claim: Some identify the whispering faculty as estimation, which assists reason in premises but retreats and begins sowing doubt when a conclusion is reached.
rows.anchor: Bazıları da demiştir ki kuvve-i vehmiyedir. Çünkü o mukaddimâtta akla müsâ‘id olur

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Alusi objects that interpreting God's speech through these faculties itself comes from the evil of the stealthy whisperer.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî’nin bunlara karşı: “Kelâmullahı böyle tefsir etmek vesvâs-ı hannâsın şerrinden olduğu hafî değildir”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Alusi's dismissal is unwarranted: excluding imagination and estimation leaves no place for whispering and neglects Satan's chief means.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî’nin bunlara karşı: “Kelâmullahı böyle tefsir etmek vesvâs-ı hannâsın şerrinden olduğu hafî değildir”[^58] diye [6425] atması da revâ olmamıştır

rows.speaker: Beyzâvî
rows.claim: Beyzawi explains the whisperer as being like the estimative faculty; the author takes this as a comparison, not an exclusion of psychological whispering.
rows.anchor: Nitekim Beyzâvî de vesvese vereni “kuvve-i vehmiye gibi” diyerek îzah etmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although whispering is connected with imagination and estimation, the author prefers the full general scope of the divine wording rather than restricting it to one faculty.
rows.anchor: şu beyân-ı ilâhînin umum ve şümûlü üzere anlamak elbette daha doğrudur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whisperer insinuates ideas into individuals' hearts and social life, particularly among the heedless, stirring bad tendencies and feelings until it diverts people from faith and leads to ruin.
rows.anchor: nâsın sînelerinde vesvese verir durur yani insanların içlerinde: gerek ferden içlerinde, gönüllerinde ve gerek cem‘iyyeten içlerinde aralarında

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina says the breast is the soul's first vehicle because the human soul first attaches to the heart and spreads through it to the other organs.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ der ki: “Nefsin birinci matıyyesi sudûrdur, zira nefs-i insânînin ilk müte‘allakı kalbdir

rows.speaker: Müfessirîn
rows.claim: Exegetes allow three parses for the relative pronoun: a genitive explanatory adjective, a nominative predicate with an implied huwa, or an accusative appositive.
rows.anchor: Müfessirîn diyorlar ki burada ٱلَّذِى mevsûlünün i‘râbında üç vecih câizdir: Birincisi, sıfat olarak mahallen mecrur olmaktır

rows.speaker: Tefsîr-i Kevâşî
rows.claim: Under the adjective parse, Kevashi says pausing at hannas is impermissible; Tibi objects that a verse-ending pause exists.
rows.anchor: Tefsîr-i Kevâşî’de “vakıf câiz olmaz” demiş, lâkin Tîbî[^62] buna “vakfın ‘adem-i cevâzında nazar vardır

rows.speaker: Keşf
rows.claim: Kashf says the pause is not necessarily beautiful when the relative clause is adjectival, except under a view that accepts a special pause at every verse ending.
rows.anchor: Keşf’te de[^63] demiştir ki “sıfat olunca hüsün müsellem değildir, meğer Allâhümme vakfı hasen bir fâsıla-i hâssada

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every Qur'anic verse ending is beautiful as a pause; one report also calls pausing at verse endings the Prophet's practice.
rows.anchor: Kur’ân’ın her fâsılası güzeldir, her âyetinde vakıf da güzel olmak lâzım gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people whose breasts are mentioned are evidently those heedless of God's remembrance, so the word may also be understood as the forgetful.
rows.anchor: Bu ٱلنَّاسِ’dan murad Allah’ı zikirden gaflet edenler, yani gaflet hâlinde olan insanlar olmak zâhirdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whisperer includes both hidden jinn and familiar human beings, and may whisper through talk about either group.
rows.anchor: Cinden ve insten yani o vesvese veren gerek gizli cin tâifesinden, cinnîlerden olsun ve gerek mâlum insanlardan

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina associates jinn with hiddenness and humans with familiarity, mapping the hidden to inward senses and the familiar to outward senses through which whispering reaches the heart.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ’nın anlayışına göre cin istitardan, ins istînastandır, umûr-ı müstetire havâss-ı bâtıne

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible sense is that whispering occurs in the breasts of both jinn and humans, leading both astray; the phrase may also mean refuge from hidden and open evil.
rows.anchor: Üçüncü bir mâna ile gerek cinden olan ve gerek insten olan nâsın sadırları içinde vesvese verir

rows.speaker: Müfessirîn
rows.claim: Exegetes offer three or four analyses of min and its attachment in the final phrase.
rows.anchor: Bunda müfessirîn üç, dört vecih zikretmişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clearest analysis makes min explanatory of the whisperer: devils come from the hidden jinn and visible human kinds, matching the account of human and jinn satans.
rows.anchor: Birincisi مِنَ beyâniye olarak الَّذِي يُوَسْوِسُ’yü beyan olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading explains the whisperer's species and establishes the need to seek God's protection from all of them.
rows.anchor: en açık mâna da budur. Ebû Zer radıyallâhu anh’tan mervîdir

rows.speaker: Ebû Zer
rows.claim: Abu Dharr asks a man whether he has sought refuge in God from a human satan.
rows.anchor: Ebû Zer radıyallâhu anh’tan mervîdir ki: Bir adama[^4]“sen Allah’a sığındın mı ins şeytanından?”[^5] demiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the second analysis, min marks the source of whispering and attaches to the verb: sometimes whispering comes from jinn, sometimes from humans.
rows.anchor: İkincisi مِنَ ibtidâiye olarak يُوَسْوِسُ’ye müte‘allik olmasıdır ki vesvese vereni değil verdiği vesvesenin mebde’ini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This source reading could let jinn include angels in a broad sense, though angels neither do evil nor whisper; deceivers can still mislead by talking about them.
rows.anchor: Bu veche göre “cin” en umûmî mânasıyla melâikeye dahi şâmil olabilir

rows.speaker: Ferrâ ve diğerleri
rows.claim: A third analysis treats the final phrase as explaining people in whose breasts whispering occurs; they say people can also refer to jinn, citing related usage.
rows.anchor: Ferrâ ve daha birtakımları buna kāil olmuşlar ve demişlerdir ki: “Nâs”, cinne de ıtlak olunur

rows.speaker: Kelbî
rows.claim: Kalbi is cited for the expression people of the jinn.
rows.anchor: Kelbî’den menkul olduğu üzere نَاسٌ مِنَ الْجِنِّ dahi denilir

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: Kashshaf rejects calling jinn people as contrary to the words' usual contrast and to Qur'anic eloquence; he prefers understanding people as the forgetful, including both groups.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf der ki: “Ben bunu doğru bulmam, çünkü cinne ‘cin’ denilmesi ictinanlarından, gizliliklerinden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls the forgetful-person reading contrary to the apparent sense and aesthetically awkward because plural breasts are attached to a singular forgetful person.
rows.anchor: bu surette “sadr”ın cem‘i olan “sudûr”un müfred olan “nâsî”ye izâfeti de zevke pek mülâyim gelmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible specialized contrast takes familiar humans as companions and jinn as hidden or unknown counterparts, with further usages extending jinn to hidden beings and dense crowds.
rows.anchor: Çünkü “ins” mutlak insan mânasına geldiği gibi, insanın ünsiyet ettiği enîsine, yâr ve hemdemi mânasına da gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This third analysis could cover all people, familiar and unknown, but is indirect, overly specialized, and leaves the more important word whisperer unexplained.
rows.anchor: Bu mâna da haddizâtında mühimdir, ve lafzın muhtemelâtından da olabilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth analysis makes the phrase explanatory of whispering or an appositive with an omitted word evil, yielding substantially the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: Dördüncü bir vecih de مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ vesvâsı beyan veya cârrın iadesi ve muzâf takdîriyle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among the proposed parses, the author judges the first the clearest: jinn indicates the metaphysical hidden domain and people the natural, visible domain, and whispering comes from either or both.
rows.anchor: Bütün bu vecihler içinde en açığı birinci vecihtir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah concludes by commanding refuge in the one God from all such harms and promising divine protection and a good end to those who seek refuge.
rows.anchor: bütün bunların şerrinden ve bâhusus vesvesesi şerrinden insanların rabbi, insanların meliki, insanların ilâhı olan Ehad, Samed Allah-ı Zü’l-celâl’e sığınmak hâtime olarak emredilmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah has 22 distinct letters, like the Opening; some take this as a hint about revelation over 22 years, though the famous report says 23.
rows.anchor: Bu sûre-i celîlenin harfleri tekrarsız olarak sayıldığında[^17] yirmi iki harftir, Fâtiha harfleri de böyledir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such apparent coincidences do not support binding doctrines or prove intended meanings, but given divine knowledge they may carry a subtle symbolic indication worth recording cautiously.
rows.anchor: bu gibi tevâfuklara ahkâm terettüb ettirilecek kadar ihticâca sâlih, ifadesi maksud bir ma‘nâ-yı murad nazarıyla bakmak doğru olmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Symbolic hints must not produce meanings contrary to clear verses or lead into Hurufism and esoteric error; subtle indications consistent with clear teaching can still enrich understanding.
rows.anchor: muhkemât hilâfına mânalar çıkarmaya kalkışmak, hurûfîlik zeyg u dalâliyle bâtınîlik zulmetlerine sürüklenmek demek olacağı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an example, the opening letter ba and final letter sin spell bes, suggesting the Qur'an is sufficient guidance containing the principles of religion, in keeping with two clear verses.
rows.anchor: Meselâ Kur’ân’ın evveli besmelenin “bâ”sı ile başladığı, âhiri de nâsın “sîn”i ile hitam bulduğu mülâhaza edilince

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Persian couplet expresses the same idea: the Qur'an begins with ba and ends with sin because it suffices as guide in both worlds.
rows.anchor: Evvel ü âhir-i Kur’an neye bâ, sîn geldi. Yani rehber iki âlemde bize Kur’an bes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar saying Allah suffices and the rest is desire makes the point more comprehensive; the author also sees resonance with the endings of al-Tawba and Ya-Sin.
rows.anchor: Bunu bizde mâruf olan “Allah bes, bâkī heves” mazmûnuyla anlamak da Kur’ân’ın evvel ü âhir bütün makāsıdını muhtevî olmak itibariyle daha cem‘iyyetli olacağını ihtar[^21] eylemek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meanings of the Opening, al-Baqara's beginning, al-Ikhlas, and the two refuge surahs themselves reveal coherence between seeking help at the start and refuge at the end.
rows.anchor: Fâtiha ve Sûre-i Bakara’nın evveli ile İhlâs ve Mu‘avvizeteyn bu üç sûrenin mâna ve mazmûnu mülâhaza edildiği zaman

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This coherence supports the author's view that the arrangement of Qur'anic surahs was revealed.
rows.anchor: bu âhenk ve tenâsüb bize Kur’an sûrelerinin tertîbi de vahiy ile olduğu hakkındaki mezhebimizin kuvvet ve isabetini gösterir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars caution against declaring meanings that arise solely from symbols to be God's intended meaning; one should seek the straight path rather than obscure routes.
rows.anchor: Onun için sırf rumûzâtından sânih[^23] olan mânalar murâd-ı ilâhî olduğuna hükmetmek doğru olmayacağı hakkında ulemânın ihtârını unutmamak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance to the straight path is the first aim for safety on Judgment Day; the final aim is full conviction and refuge in God's lordship, sovereignty, and divinity, which bring ultimate human happiness and a good end.
rows.anchor: insanlığın gāye-i saâdeti îkān ile ittikādadır, hüsn-i hâtime onunladır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who act according to the perfect Book's guidance reach the good end by God's grace, and people must ask for it through the Fatiha covenant and seek refuge with certainty and sincerity.
rows.anchor: Bize düşen إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ mîsâkıyla O’nu istemek ve îkān ü ihlâs ile O’na sığınmaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In his closing prayer, the author asks for himself, his nation, and fellow believers to be freed from whisperings and granted sound hearts, upright consciences, and a blessed end.
rows.anchor: hem kendim hem milletim, ihvân-ı dînim hakkında vesveselerden âzâde kalb-i selîm ve vicdân-ı müstakīm ile o âkıbet-i hüsnâya tevfîkini diler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He recalls spending twelve years, day and night, writing the Qur'an's translation and commentary, weeping over his sixty-year life, and signs off with Allah suffices, the rest is desire.
rows.anchor: on iki seneden beri gece ve gündüz aşk-ı Hak ile, gözlerinden nokta be-nokta eşk-i revân dökerek altmış senelik sahîfe-i hayâtıma

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The colophon marks Hamdi's Qur'an commentary as complete and dates it 12 Jumada al-Akhira 1357, corresponding to 8 August 1938.
rows.anchor: Elhamdülillâh Hamdi tamâm bu
